title: Website Updates (Feb 2026)
text:
Wider sidebar: Increased from ~200px to 260px for better prominence
Better centering: Added 80px left margin to content area for improved balance
Responsive: Layout adjusts appropriately on mobile devices





Added comprehensive meta descriptions to all pages
Configured Open Graph and Twitter Card tags for social sharing
Added structured keywords for search engines
Enabled sitemap generation
Added site-url configuration for proper indexing
Set up Google Analytics placeholder (update with your GA4 ID)





Created markdown-based CV in ../cv/ directory
Supports multiple output formats:

HTML (for web viewing)
PDF (for download, matches current CV style)
LaTeX (can export if needed)

Build script (cv/build_cv.sh) generates all formats
Easy to maintain - edit one markdown file, get all formats





From the website/ directory:
quarto render
This will regenerate all HTML files in the docs/ folder.



From the cv/ directory:
./build_cv.sh
This creates HTML and PDF versions of the CV.



The site is configured for GitHub Pages. After making changes:
cd website/
quarto render
cd docs/
git add .
git commit -m "Update website"
git push



To create a page that’s not in the sidebar menu:

Create a .qmd file in the website directory (e.g., hidden-page.qmd)
Don’t add it to _quarto.yml sidebar contents
The page will be accessible at /hidden-page.html but won’t appear in navigation

To make it truly hidden from search engines, add to the page YAML:
---
title: "Hidden Page"
robots: noindex, nofollow
---



To enable analytics: 1. Get your Google Analytics 4 (GA4) measurement ID 2. In _quarto.yml, replace "G-XXXXXXXXXX" with your actual ID



A sitemap is automatically generated at docs/sitemap.xml when you render the site. Submit this to: - Google Search Console - Bing Webmaster Tools




Build and preview the updated site
If satisfied, commit and push changes
Set up Google Analytics (optional)
Submit sitemap to search engines
Consider adding a robots.txt file if needed

title: Research
text:
The Demand for Elections under Autocracy: Regime Approval and the Elimination of Local Elections in Russia (with Quintin Beazer and Ora John Reuter) American Journal of Political Science, 2024


Abstract

Why do some authoritarian regimes hold elections while others do not? We argue that regime approval shapes the decision to cancel elections.


Endogenous Popularity: How Perceptions of Regime Support Affect the Popularity of Authoritarian Regimes (with Kyle Marquardt, Ora John Reuter, and Ekaterina Tertytchnaya) American Political Science Review, 2024, 118(2):1046-1052 DOI


Abstract

Do perceptions of a regime’s popularity affect actual support for it? Using survey experiments in Russia, we show that information about the regime’s popularity causally increases support for it.


Staying Out of Trouble: Criminal Cases Against Russian Mayors (with Ora John Reuter, Michael Rochlitz, and Anton Aisin) Comparative Political Studies, 2022, 55(9):1539-1568


Abstract

Why are some local officials prosecuted while others are not? We examine criminal cases against Russian mayors.


Who Reports Crime? Citizen Engagement with the Police in Russia and Georgia (with Timothy Frye, Scott Gehlbach, and Lauren McCarthy) Europe-Asia Studies, 2021, 73(1):8-35

Performance Incentives under Autocracy: Evidence from Russia’s Regions (with Ora John Reuter) Comparative Politics, 2019, 51(2):239-266


Abstract

We find that performance-based appointments are more frequent in less competitive regions. In more competitive regions, the political imperatives of maintaining a political machine may lead regime leaders to abandon cadre policies that promote economic development.


Staring at the West through Kremlin-tinted Glasses: Russian Mass and Elite Divergence in Attitudes toward the United States, European Union, and Ukraine before and after Crimea (with Joshua A. Tucker) Post-Soviet Affairs, 2019, 35(5-6):365-375

Local Elections in Authoritarian Regimes: An Elite-Based Theory with Evidence from Russian Mayoral Elections (with Ora John Reuter, Guzel Garifullina, and Alexandra Shubenkova) Comparative Political Studies, 2016, 49(5)


Abstract

We argue that autocrats use subnational elections to co-opt and assuage powerful subnational elites. When subnational elites control significant political resources, leaders may need to co-opt them in order to govern cost-effectively.


Cooperating with the State: Evidence from Survey Experiments on Policing (with Timothy Frye, Scott Gehlbach, and Lauren McCarthy) Journal of Experimental Political Science, 2016, 3(2):124-139

The Political Economy of Russian Gubernatorial Elections and Appointments (with Timothy Frye, Guzel Garifullina, and Ora John Reuter) Europe-Asia Studies, 2014, 66(8)

Elections, Appointments, and Human Capital: The Case of Russian Mayors (with Guzel Garifullina, Ora John Reuter, and Alexandra Shubenkova) Demokratizatsiya, 2014, 22(1)

title: Noah Buckley - Political Scientist
text:
Assistant Professor of Political Science


Department of Political Science, Trinity College Dublin


Email · Google Scholar · SSRN
I am an assistant professor (with tenure) in the Department of Political Science at Trinity College Dublin. I received my Ph.D. from Columbia University in 2016 and was previously a postdoctoral associate at NYU Abu Dhabi.
My research focuses on authoritarian politics in Putin-era Russia: how autocratic regimes sustain themselves, how the mass public understands their authoritarian environment, and why corruption persists. I use quantitative methods and original micro-level data, including the largest individual-level database of Russian public opinion survey responses.
My work has appeared in the American Political Science Review, American Journal of Political Science, Comparative Political Studies, Comparative Politics, Journal of Experimental Political Science, Europe-Asia Studies, and Post-Soviet Affairs.
(Looking for Noah M. Buckley-Farlee? That’s me.)

title: Claude Code for Political Scientists
text:
I’ve been telling everyone I know about Claude Code and figured I should write something down instead of cornering people at conferences. If you’re curious, skeptical, or just wondering what I won’t shut up about, this is for you.
The short version: it has helped me do literally months of RA work in a few weeks. I think it will change the field quickly, in good and bad and unexpected ways. I gave a demo to a skeptical friend the other day and converted him instantly.

title: Claude Code for Political Scientists
text:
So what is it?
You open a terminal in your project folder, describe what you want in plain English, and an AI agent reads your files, writes code, runs it, looks at the output, fixes its mistakes, and iterates. You watch—or go make coffee and come back to finished work.
It’s not a chatbot you paste code into. It lives inside your project. It can see your directory structure, read your data files, and remember context across a conversation. Less “AI autocomplete,” more “RA who reads fast, codes fast, and never sleeps.”

title: Claude Code for Political Scientists
section: What I’ve actually used it for
text:
What I’ve actually used it for
Most discussion of AI coding tools is aimed at software engineers. We have different problems—messy data, weird file formats, legacy code from 2014 that nobody wants to touch. Turns out it’s good at exactly this kind of thing.
Roughly in order of how much it’s changed my life:
Cleaning and harmonizing data. I work with decades of Russian survey data across dozens of waves—different formats, inconsistent variable names, coding schemes that change over time, column headers in Cyrillic that sometimes look like Latin characters but aren’t. This is exactly the tedious, detail-oriented work that used to eat weeks. Claude Code does it well and fast.
Building whole analysis pipelines. I had precinct-level election data for 12 Russian elections and wanted to implement a bunch of fraud detection methods. I described what I needed, and over a few sessions it built the entire pipeline—data loading, a dozen statistical tests, validation against published estimates, export to a panel dataset, publication figures. The kind of project I’d budget a full semester for.
Scraping and data collection. It has enabled me to collect data that I didn’t think was possible without a very technical RA—web scraping, processing government budget documents in inconsistent Excel formats across years, API work.
Rebooting stalled papers. This one’s my favorite. I wrote a custom command that I point at a project folder—maybe it has years of accumulated code, old drafts, emails from coauthors, reviewer comments sitting in a stuff/ folder. Claude reads everything, builds a clean replication pipeline, inventories what data I have across my other projects, and writes up a prioritized to-do list. You go from “I can’t face reopening this” to a clean, running pipeline in a few hours. For someone with multiple papers in various stages of dormancy (i.e., everyone), this is genuinely transformative.
Simulations and methods. A colleague asked about a methodological question. I described the simulation, went to do other things, came back to complete Monte Carlo results with figures. Maybe three hours elapsed, very little of it mine.
The unglamorous stuff. Regression tables, figures, codebooks, Stata exports. It does all of this quickly and saves you the time you’d spend on Stack Overflow remembering modelsummary options.

title: Claude Code for Political Scientists
text:
Where it falls short
Interpretation. Tom Pepinsky nails it: “Use agentic AI for tasks that involve following rules. Do not use agentic AI for tasks that generate answers, arguments, or interpretations.” It can run your regressions; you still have to know what they mean.
Citations. It makes them up. Don’t ask it for literature reviews.
Knowing when your design is wrong. It will cheerfully implement whatever you ask for, including bad ideas. You’re still the researcher.
If your work is mostly clean experiments. The gains are biggest when there’s a lot of messy data wrangling. If you run pre-registered survey experiments with tidy datasets, you’ll still find it useful, but less life-changing.

title: Claude Code for Political Scientists
text:
The “academic slop” worry
Seva Gunitsky raises a real concern: if competent empirical work becomes cheap, we’ll drown in technically adequate but pointless papers. I think about this a lot, and he’s right to worry.
My take: the tool amplifies what you bring to it. Good questions and careful instincts? It removes the barriers to pursuing them. Bad questions? You produce bad papers faster. The bottleneck moves from execution to judgment—which, honestly, is where it always should have been.

title: Claude Code for Political Scientists
text:
Getting started
Install it. You need a Claude Max subscription ($100/month, easiest option) or an Anthropic API key. Then:
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
Open a terminal in any project folder and type claude.
Start small. Clean a dataset you’ve been avoiding. Make a figure. Reformat a regression table. Don’t try to build an entire pipeline on day one.
Write a CLAUDE.md file. This is the single most important trick. It’s a plain text file in your project that Claude reads at the start of every session. Put your coding preferences, project structure, data locations, and rules in there. I have strong feelings about R style (base R, explicit loops, no pipes) and it follows them reliably once they’re written down. Think of it as onboarding an RA.
Verify everything. Same discipline you’d apply to RA work. Check output, run the code yourself, look at the data. It’s tempting to skip this because the tool is fast. Don’t. Scott Cunningham’s “Referee 2 protocol”—opening a second Claude instance to adversarially audit the first—is a clever approach.

title: Claude Code for Political Scientists
text:
Further reading

Scott Cunningham on Claude Code for empirical research — best resource I’ve found for social scientists. His whole series is worth reading.
Tom Pepinsky, “Agentic AI and Social Science Research Practice” — clear-eyed on what it’s good and bad at.
Seva Gunitsky, “The Age of Academic Slop Is Upon Us” — the risks. Read this alongside any enthusiasm.
Claude Code docs — official documentation, more geared toward developers but the basics transfer.


Happy to give a live demo anytime. Seeing is believing.
